segments.text_en: Mellow Math · Flow God Plays Dice A century ago, physicists discovered that the universe is not a clockwork — it is a casino. This is the story of how certainty died, and what replaced it. Begin

segments.text_en: Chapter 0 The experiment that shattered reality In 1801, Thomas Young passed light through two narrow slits and saw something impossible: an interference pattern — proof that light is a wave. A century later, physicists repeated the experiment firing one photon at a time . Each photon landed as a single dot. But as thousands accumulated, the interference pattern emerged again. A single particle, somehow interfering with itself .

A century later, physicists repeated the experiment firing one photon at a time . Each photon landed as a single dot. But as thousands accumulated, the interference pattern emerged again. segments.text_en: Chapter 1 The universe was perfect For two hundred years, physics was a triumph of certainty. Newton's laws could predict the motion of every planet, every cannonball, every grain of sand — if you knew the starting conditions. The universe was a clockwork machine , and the laws of physics were its gears. drag a ball and release to shoot — watch perfect Newtonian mechanics Every collision obeys conservation of momentum and energy exactly. No surprises. No randomness.

The universe was a clockwork machine , and the laws of physics were its gears. 공을 드래그하고 놓아 발사하세요 — 완벽한 뉴턴 역학 Every collision obeys conservation of momentum and energy exactly. No surprises. segments.text_en: Chapter 2 The oven that broke physics In 1859, Gustav Kirchhoff posed a challenge: determine the spectrum of light emitted by a heated cavity. By the 1890s, experimentalists had mapped the curve precisely. But no theory could explain it. Classical physics made a terrifying prediction. The Rayleigh–Jeans law — derived honestly from Maxwell's electromagnetism and Boltzmann's thermodynamics — said that the energy radiated should grow without bound at high frequencies.

segments.text_en: Chapter 3 The more you know, the less you know Imagine trying to locate an electron. You shine light on it. But light carries momentum — to see something small, you need short-wavelength (high-energy) light, which kicks the electron unpredictably. Use gentle long-wavelength light, and you cannot see where it is. This was Heisenberg's gamma-ray microscope thought experiment, published in 1927. But the uncertainty principle goes deeper than clumsy measurements.
segments.text_ko: Chapter 3 더 많이 알수록, 더 적게 알게 된다 Imagine trying to locate an electron. You shine light on it. But light carries momentum — to see something small, you need short-wavelength (high-energy) light, which kicks the electron unpredictably. Use gentle long-wavelength light, and you cannot see where it is. This was Heisenberg's gamma-ray microscope thought experiment, published in 1927. But the uncertainty principle goes deeper than clumsy measurements. It is not that we disturb the particle by looking.

segments.text_en: Chapter 4 A coin that is both Imagine flipping a coin that is, genuinely, both heads and tails at once — not because you haven't looked, but because it has no single value until you do. A quantum particle in a superposition does not simply have an unknown state. It exists in all possible states simultaneously. When we measure, the superposition collapses to a single definite outcome. In 1922, Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach sent silver atoms through an inhomogeneous magnetic field.

segments.text_en: Chapter 5 Spooky action at a distance In May 1935, Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen published a paper with an innocent title and an explosive argument. Two particles, once entangled, remain correlated no matter how far apart. Measure one — the other's state is instantly determined. Einstein saw only two options: either information travels faster than light (impossible), or the particles always "knew" their values in advance through hidden variables .
segments.text_ko: Chapter 5 으스스한 원격 작용 In May 1935, Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen published a paper with an innocent title and an explosive argument. Two particles, once entangled, remain correlated no matter how far apart. Measure one — the other's state is instantly determined. Einstein saw only two options: either information travels faster than light (impossible), or the particles always "knew" their values in advance through hidden variables . He concluded quantum mechanics must be incomplete.

segments.text_en: Chapter 6 What does it all mean ? Quantum mechanics is, by any measure, the most successful theory in the history of science. It predicts the behavior of atoms, molecules, semiconductors, lasers, and nuclear reactions with staggering accuracy. But after a century, physicists still cannot agree on what the theory says about reality . The fight began at the fifth Solvay Conference in October 1927 — perhaps the most extraordinary gathering of minds in history.
